It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing a world where “earthly kingdoms go the way of all flesh” through the perversion of justice, and I must ask you with a gentle heart: why do you ask after God’s response to corrupt legal systems in this hour? [13, 19, 20, 1503, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” by the sight of “savage wolves” who use human law as a “scourge” against the faithful, or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that the Master “sovereignly orders everything He has made”—including the rise and fall of every unjust court? [13, 20, 54, 1143, 1374, 1425, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to find “diplomatic relations” with a culture that “mocks, vilifies, and censures” the Scriptures, we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs the “record of history” by promising that His justice will never fail [11, 28, 120, 121, 219, 1197, 1503, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, the existence of “weaponized legal persecution” is not an “administrative anomaly” but is subject to the “decree from God” who “raises up kings, then pulls them from their thrones when they have served His administration” [15, 68, 533, 1143, 1392, 1532, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The God Who Hears the Cry of the Oppressed (Egypt)**

**Verse**
“ ‘And the LORD said: “I have surely seen the oppression of My people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters, for I know their sorrows. So I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up from that land to a good and large land, to a land flowing with milk and honey” ’ ” (Exodus 3:7–8). [1192, 1231, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Scriptures reveal that God is not “remote and uninvolved” but is a “loving, beneficent Father” who “heard their groaning” and “remembered His covenant” when the “legalized” oppression of the taskmasters became too heavy (Exodus 2:24) [11, 15, 1194, 1208, Conversation History]. Reformed theology—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that “Egypt, the world power of its day, was systematically dismantled under the breathtaking wrath of God” because the Lord “demands a reckoning” for the mistreatment of those He has “bought” (Exodus 32:6; Genesis 9:5) [11, 261, 962, 1207, Conversation History]. This proves that “nothing thwarts any aspect of His plan,” as the Lord uses even the “bitter... bondage” of an unjust state to “show My power in you, and that My name may be declared in all the earth” (Exodus 1:14; 9:16) [5, 11, 21, 1196, 1202, 1315, 1572, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “trade in your worry for trust,” for “the LORD will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace,” knowing that He “responds to the prayer of the destitute” (Exodus 14:14; Psalm 102:17) [94, 201, 1197, 1211, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. Recognize that “he who trusts in his own heart is a fool,” and you must instead “tremble at My word” which promised that “the LORD was with Joseph” even when he was a “victim of injustice” and “unjustly accused” (Genesis 39:2; 50:20) [11, 500, 501, 858, 1313, 1406, 1503, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **theocratic context**, the Exodus was the “beginning of the fulfillment” of the national promise to Abraham, where “national greatness” was a “temporal sign” of God’s favor [409, 1188, 1313, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “victory,” showing that our “redemption” is not merely from physical taskmasters but from the “bondage of sin,” for our “citizenship is in heaven” and our “federal head” is Christ, not an earthly monarch (Philippians 3:20; Romans 5:12–21) [13, 26, 32, 38, 142, 440, 445, 1203, 1313, 1320, 1426, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: The Divine Rebuke of Corrupt Courts (Prophets and Law)**

**Verse**
“ ‘He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the just, Both of them alike are an abomination to the LORD’ ” (Proverbs 17:15). [170, 236, Conversation History]. “ ‘Keep yourself far from a false matter; do not kill the innocent and righteous. For I will not justify the wicked’ ” (Exodus 23:7). [170, 511, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The “record of history” shows that God “abominates” any legal system where “justice never goes forth” and “perverse judgment proceeds” because “the wicked surround the righteous” (Habakkuk 1:4) [11, 15, 1104, 1532, 1720, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition—upheld by **Voddie Baucham**—teaches that “the judgment is God’s,” and therefore human judges who “rule by their own power” and “take a bribe” will ultimately be “weighed on the scales and found deficient” (Deuteronomy 1:17; Daniel 5:27; Jeremiah 5:31) [37, 314, 427, 1061, 1112, 1129, 1130, 1143, 1402, 1720, Conversation History]. The prophets warned that those who “rip open the women with child” or “pervert the justice of all the afflicted” would face a “hot” divine wrath that “will not at all acquit the wicked” (Amos 1:13; Proverbs 31:5; Nahum 1:3) [170, 631, 729, 1056, 1201, 1317, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You must “discipline your mind” to “not follow a crowd to do evil” or “testify in a dispute so as to... pervert justice” (Exodus 23:2) [90, 116, 510, 1202, 1406, 1515, 1709, Conversation History]. “Wait for His Son from heaven,” for though “the kings of the earth set themselves... against the LORD,” He who “sits in the heavens shall laugh” and “break them with a rod of iron” (Psalm 2:2–4, 9) [11, 14, 24, 94, 109, 201, 803, 804, 1315, 1408, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Civil vs. Divine Decrees**
Under the **Mosaic Law**, “testifying in a dispute” required “two or three witnesses” to prevent “unrighteous” convictions, yet the Israelites often “forgot the LORD” and “corrupted all their deeds” (Deuteronomy 17:6; Zephaniah 3:7) [544, 582, 1104, 1140, 1317, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “warfare,” teaching that while we “do not wrestle against flesh and blood,” we must use the “sword of the Spirit” to “cast down arguments” that “deny the only Lord God” (Ephesians 6:12; 2 Corinthians 10:4–5; Jude 4) [13, 21, 32, 43, 92, 113, 201, 1081, 1313, 1325, 1408, 1415, 1440, 1479, 1515, 1520, 1601, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: The King and Apostles Before the Sanhedrin (Jesus and the Church)**

**Verse**
“ ‘Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If My kingdom were of this world, My servants would fight, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but now My kingdom is not from here” ’ ” (John 18:36). [18, 1296, 1431, 1529, Conversation History]. “ ‘But Peter and the other apostles answered and said: “We ought to obey God rather than men” ’ ” (Acts 5:29). [48, 875, 914, 1074, 1130, 1176, 1205, 1247, 1249, 1256, 1300, 1431, 1529, 1720, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Scripture records that the “Great Sanhedrin” was “riddled with injustice and corruption,” conspiring to “murder” the Son of God to maintain their “political status” [130, 205, 1124, 1422, 1720, Conversation History]. Christ’s trial before Pilate and the Sanhedrin revealed that “the religious leaders’ blind hatred was such that they frankly did not care” about truth, yet Jesus “committed Himself to Him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23) [110, 1062, 1313, 1404, 1515, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition—echoed by **Paul Washer**—notes that “the worst atrocity ever carried out”—the death of the innocent Lamb—was subject to the “determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God” to “save many people alive” (Acts 2:23; Genesis 50:20) [5, 501, 1132, 1315, 1431, 1503, 1567, Conversation History]. When the apostles were commanded to cease preaching, they established the “binding and authoritative mandate” that the church must “refuse to yield submission” to any state that usurps the “exclusive headship” of Christ [11, 15, 19, 68, 1092, 1130, 1144, 1316, 1431, 1528, 1627, 1636, 1638, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “be bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God in much conflict,” for “the word of God is not chained” (1 Thessalonians 2:2; 2 Timothy 2:9) [51, 76, 91, 123, 767, 1081, 1406, 1420, 1431, 1461, 1503, 1504, 1646, 1670, 1720, Conversation History]. Recognize that “your life is not your own,” and you must “discipline your body” to “stand fast in the faith, be brave, be strong” (1 Corinthians 6:19; 16:13) [11, 12, 13, 101, 116, 169, 1056, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1502, 1515, 1670, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Civil Authority vs. Sanctuary**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, “cities of refuge” protected the slayer from “private justice,” showing God’s care for “due process” even in a primitive age [572, 1036, 1048, 1274, 1313, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** the call to submission, showing that while we are “subject to the governing authorities” in secular matters, we must “obey God rather than men” when human law “tampers with or attempt[s] to tone down the gospel” (Romans 13:1; Acts 5:29) [15, 19, 75, 1130, 1144, 1184, 1246, 1284, 1316, 1342, 1422, 1473, 1532, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Hope and Duty of the Persecuted Today**

**Verse**
“ ‘And shall God not avenge His own elect who cry out day and night to Him, though He bears long with them? I tell you that He will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He really find faith on the earth?’ ” (Luke 18:7–8). [203, 220, 222, Conversation History]. “ ‘And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain, for the former things have passed away’ ” (Revelation 21:4). [14, 201, 332, 452, 453, 468, 470, 816, 940, 948, 1315, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture handles the “noise and tumult” of weaponized law by fixating on the “consummation of history,” where “Christ ultimately crushes the kingdoms of men and establishes His own” [13, 16, 20, 21, 23, 24, 31, 35, 103, 136, 1199, 1311, 1315, 1503, 1515, 1524, 1532, 1636, 1720, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition asserts that the “church militant” is called to “contend earnestly for the faith,” which includes “snatching them out of the fire” of deception and “seeking justice” for the vulnerable (Jude 3, 23; Isaiah 1:17) [160, 391, 664, 760, 1137, 1141, 1246, 1290, 1316, 1349, 1358, 1389, 1408, 1425, 1440, 1461, 1463, 1503, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. Our hope is not in “human court[s]” or “political maneuvering,” but in the “Lord, the righteous Judge,” who will “render vengeance to My enemies” (Psalm 94:19; 1 Corinthians 4:3; Deuteronomy 32:41) [11, 32, 35, 37, 63, 201, 328, 455, 789, 852, 948, 976, 1233, 1315, 1408, 1460, 1515, 1684, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptations” and His “everlasting dominion” is “secure” (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 2 Peter 2:9; Daniel 7:14) [11, 14, 24, 47, 92, 94, 109, 121, 147, 176, 201, 352, 412, 602, 630, 852, 869, 948, 957, 1132, 1138, 1143, 1313, 1315, 1408, 1420, 1450, 1515, 1572, 1720, Conversation History]. Find “tranquility of soul” by “resting upon the surest foundation,” for “He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6) [5, 11, 24, 47, 92, 94, 102, 113, 121, 147, 176, 192, 201, 313, 315, 352, 412, 442, 630, 829, 830, 920, 1012, 1132, 1138, 1143, 1408, 1420, 1445, 1450, 1515, 1572, 1720, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 87, 147, 176, 211, 222, 285, 291, 300, 313, 324, 332, 361, 405, 413, 414, 444, 449, 591, 834, 1138, 1407, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

references.cited_text: As a Father Who Requires Obedience Because God was their Father, the people were required to obey Him. Deuteronomy 32:6 reiterates that: “Do you thus repay the LORD, O foolish and unwise people? Is not He your Father who has bought you?” The Biblical Perspective of God When Jesus arrived on the scene, He reintroduced His Jewish audience to God as a loving, beneficent Father to those who know, love, and obey Him. In the Sermon on the Mount, He taught them that the Father takes care of the needs of His children:

Let’s look at a specific example from the book of Job. In the midst of terrible suffering, Job tragically compounded his anguish by doing what he should have learned never to do: He contested God’s wisdom, expressly resenting what the mighty hand of God had brought him. Take time to sense the raw human emotion seething under the words of his lament: I cry out to you, O God, but you do not answer; I stand up, but you merely look at me. You turn on me ruthlessly; with the might of your hand you attack me. You snatch me up and drive me before the wind; you toss me about in the storm. I know you will bring me down to death. (Job 30:20–23 NIV)

[W]hat does the Lord require of you But to do justly, To love mercy, And to walk humbly with your God? He would be fully aware that “whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will also cry himself and not be heard” (Prov. 21:13). The principle spelled out in James 2:13 was woven into the Old Testament as well: “Judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy.” The priest was surely familiar with Exodus 23:4–5: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, and you would refrain from helping it, you shall surely help him with it.” So if a person found his enemy’s donkey in a ditch, he was obliged to rescue the donkey, right? Of course he had a greater duty to help a man in critical condition.

Did you ever wonder why Jesus preached law instead of grace to them? In neither case did He go on to give the gospel’s answer to the eternally important question those men raised. Why? Because the law was what they needed to hear. Neither man had ever truly felt the weight of the law. They did not believe themselves to be lost. “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. [Jesus] did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance” (Mark 2:17). The gospel has nothing to say to people who are satisfied with their own righteousness. There is no truly good news for someone in that state of mind.

Jesus built this illustration around a widow because as far as the Old Testament goes, her case ought to have been clear-cut. Regardless of the legal merits of her claim, the judge should have done something to care for her purely on the grounds of mercy. Moses’ law was explicit on this point. God Himself said, “You shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child. If you afflict them in any way, and they cry at all to Me, I will surely hear their cry; and My wrath will become hot, and I will kill you with the sword; your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless” (Ex. 22:22–24). The principle is echoed in Isaiah 1:17:

Here’s proof that the parable of the unjust judge pertains to the Second Coming, urging us to pray faithfully and persistently for that day. The end of Luke 18:8 is the key: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He really find faith on the earth?” Will He find His people persevering in prayer and expectation? Or will many “lose heart”? The parable is an encouragement to hold fast and keep praying. The widow in this parable represents all true Christians— the elect. We are, in a sense, helpless—“poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3); “not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble” (1 Cor. 1:26). We are totally at the mercy of the Judge.

Adoption and the Old Testament As we saw in the previous chapter, the New Testament doctrine of adoption begins to come alive when we understand the legal proceedings of first-century Rome. But, as with the slavery metaphor, we must also consider the history of ancient Israel, recognizing the theological backdrop that the Old Testament provides for the New Testament. In so doing, we will discover a profound richness that is added to our understanding of the biblical imagery. One of the first adoptions recorded in the Old Testament was that of Moses,3 whose life was spared when his mother floated him down the Nile River in a waterproof basket. When Pharaoh’s daughter came to the river and found him, she took pity on him. Miriam—Moses’ sister, who had been watching from nearby—offered to find a suitable nursemaid for the baby, and Pharaoh’s daughter agreed. As a result, Moses was returned to his birth mother until he was old enough to go live in the palace. At that time, he was brought to “Pharaoh’s daughter and he became her son” (Ex. 2:10). Thus, Moses—the son of slaves— became part of the royal family of Egypt (cf. Acts 7:20–21).

The implications are hard to miss—especially in light of the first-century slave/master imagery on which the story is built. The Master is currently away, but He will be returning soon.6 Opportunity abounds, but time is running out. When He arrives, He will judge His slaves. Those who have demonstrated faithfulness to Him (thereby evidencing the genuineness of their conversion) will be rewarded with His pleasure and welcomed into heaven. Those who have squandered every resource (thereby evidencing the true condition of their hard hearts) will receive divine condemnation and punishment.

We are no longer subject to our sinful passions; now we are subjects of our heavenly King. He is simultaneously our Master, our Patron, our Father, and our sovereign Prince.

Having been regenerated by grace apart from works, believers eagerly desire to follow Christ (1 Thess. 1:6), and the Holy Spirit enables them to do just that. Thus, it is their profound joy, through the power of the Spirit, “to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live sensibly, righteously and godly in the present age” (Titus 2:12 nasb).
